newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka diesel imports to rise as rains fail.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka diesel imports to rise as rains fail.

text.p: Sri Lanka will increase diesel imports this year to meet rising power generation demands and avoid power cuts as drought threatens to dry up hydropower reservoirs, officials said on Tuesday.
An official of the state-owned Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) said Sri Lanka planned to import 700,000 tonnes of diesel this year.

"We plan to increase gas oil (diesel) imports to 700,000 tonnes this year to meet increased power generation because of drought and also because our production is lower because of the 40-day refinery shutdown," said the official, who declined to be identified.
The Indian Ocean island imported 600,000 tonnes of diesel last year, up from the planned 300,000 tonnes because of a drought, he said.
The CPC's only refinery at Sapugaskanda, just north of Colombo, which can process 50-60,000 barrels per day, reopened last week after a routine maintenance shutdown.

The Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) state power utility chairman Arjun Deraniyagala said in January the CEB was urgently increasing thermal power generation to ride out a drought caused by the failure of northeast monsoon rains for the second straight year.
He said the utility was confident of avoiding power cuts, which disrupted commerce and industry last year, by increasing output.
The CEB would cut dependence on hydropower to 57 percent of the total requirement by building more thermal power plants by June this year, Deraniyagala said.
The government has asked the private sector to set up diesel generating plants and sell electricity to the CEB to augment emergency supply.
The island now has an installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power, produced mainly by diesel plants.

Water levels in hydropower reservoirs, which supply 85 percent of the electricity, have fallen to dangerously low levels with the failure of the November-March northeast monsoon for the second consecutive year, and weak intermonsoon showers.
The Indian Ocean island has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectric plants, usually starts around the third week of May.

"The situation is a bit hairy but we can manage for now," said a senior CEB official, who declined to be identified. "Our storage now is 436 gigawatt hours (GwH), about 35 percent of our installed storage capacity of 1,260 GwH."
He said an extra 145 megawatts would be added to the national grid by private-sector generators until the CEB's new diesel plants with 155 megawatts capacity are commissioned in June.
"But if these stop-gap measures do not come on stream as planned (because of environmental reasons) there could be problems," he said.
An 11.2 megawatt generator operated by the private sector in a Colombo suburb was shut down recently after residents complained it made too much noise.
